plan_a_advantages: Plan A has more rest days, which could be beneficial for a runner prone to injury or those new to training.
The simplicity of Plan A might be easier to adhere to for some individuals.
The focus on form and cadence during easy runs in Plan A is a good habit to reinforce.
plan_b_advantages: Plan B includes dedicated hill workouts, crucial for trail running speed and strength.
The higher training volume in Plan B likely leads to greater physiological adaptations.
The threshold intensity hill sessions will improve lactate threshold, a key determinant of running speed.
Plan B incorporates a better balance of hard and easy efforts, promoting both development and recovery.
reasoning: While both plans incorporate rest days, Plan B appears to be a more effective approach to becoming a faster trail runner. The inclusion of dedicated hill sessions, performed at a threshold intensity, directly addresses a key component of trail running performance: climbing strength and power. Plan A focuses solely on easy runs, which, while important for building aerobic base, doesn't adequately target the specific demands of trail running. The higher total training volume in Plan B also suggests a greater stimulus for adaptation and improvement.
